lesson.title: JavaScript Scope, Hoisting and Closures
objectives: Explain global, function and block scope and how the scope chain resolves a variable.
Describe hoisting for var, let, const, function declarations and the temporal dead zone.
Define a closure and explain why an inner function keeps access to outer variables.
Use closures for private state, factories and once/memoize helpers.
Predict the output of the classic loop-with-setTimeout interview question.
lesson.definition: Scope is the set of rules that decides where a variable can be accessed. JavaScript uses lexical scope: a function can see the variables of the place where it was written, not where it is called. A closure is a function bundled with references to the variables of its surrounding scope, so it can keep reading and updating them even after the outer function has returned.

theory.heading: Three kinds of scope and the scope chain
theory.body: Variables declared at the top level of a script are global. Variables declared with var inside a function are function-scoped. Variables declared with let and const are block-scoped: they exist only inside the nearest pair of braces, such as an if block or a for loop. When code reads a name, the engine looks in the current scope, then the enclosing scope, and so on up to the global scope. This lookup path is the scope chain, and it is fixed by where the code is written (lexical scope).
points: var: function-scoped, can be redeclared, attaches to window in non-module browser scripts.
let: block-scoped, can be reassigned, cannot be redeclared in the same scope.
const: block-scoped and cannot be reassigned, but an object it points to can still be mutated.
An inner scope can read outer variables; an outer scope cannot read inner ones.

theory.heading: Hoisting and the temporal dead zone
theory.body: Before running a scope, the engine registers every declaration in it. Function declarations are registered with their full body, so they can be called before the line that defines them. var declarations are registered and initialised to undefined. let, const and class declarations are registered but not initialised; reading them before the declaration line throws a ReferenceError. The region between the start of the block and the declaration is called the temporal dead zone (TDZ). The TDZ exists to catch bugs where a value is used before it is ready.
points: console.log(a); var a = 1; prints undefined.
console.log(b); let b = 1; throws ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization.
Function expressions and arrow functions assigned to variables follow the variable's hoisting rules, not function hoisting.

theory.heading: What a closure really is
theory.body: Every function object keeps a hidden link to the lexical environment in which it was created. When the outer function returns, its local variables are not destroyed if an inner function still references them; the garbage collector keeps them alive. The inner function therefore has persistent, private state. Closures capture variables, not values: if the variable changes later, the closure sees the new value.
points: Each call of the outer function creates a fresh environment, so two counters from the same factory do not share state.
Closures power module patterns, event handlers, React hooks, debounce/throttle and middleware factories in Express.
A closure that holds a large object (for example a DOM node or a big array) keeps it in memory, which can cause leaks.

theory.heading: The loop and setTimeout question
theory.body: With var, a for loop has one shared variable i for all iterations. Callbacks scheduled with setTimeout run after the loop has finished, so they all read the final value. With let, the specification creates a new binding of i for each iteration, so each callback closes over its own copy. Before let existed, developers fixed this with an IIFE that passed i as a parameter, creating a new scope per iteration.
points: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); prints 3, 3, 3.
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); prints 0, 1, 2.
Explaining per-iteration bindings is what separates a strong answer from a memorised one.

theory.heading: Practical closure patterns
theory.body: Interviewers often ask you to implement a small utility with closures. once(fn) runs fn the first time and returns the cached result afterwards. memoize(fn) keeps a cache object in the closure. A rate limiter or counter factory hides its count so callers can change it only through the returned methods. In Node, Express middleware factories such as requireRole('admin') return a function that closes over the role argument.
points: Data privacy: state is reachable only through the returned functions.
Configuration: a factory captures settings once and returns a specialised function.
Caching: memoization stores computed results keyed by the arguments.

example.title: A counter factory with private state
example.body: makeCounter returns three functions that all close over the same count variable. Code outside cannot set count directly, which is the essence of encapsulation with closures. Calling makeCounter again creates an independent count.

use_cases.title: Express middleware factories
use_cases.description: requireRole('admin') returns (req, res, next) => {...} that remembers the required role through a closure.

use_cases.title: React hooks and event handlers
use_cases.description: Handlers defined inside a component close over the props and state of that render, which explains the stale-closure bug in useEffect.

use_cases.title: Debounce and throttle
use_cases.description: The timer id is stored in a closure so repeated calls can cancel or skip the previous one, for example in a search box.

use_cases.title: Memoization and caching
use_cases.description: A cache object kept in a closure avoids repeating expensive work such as formatting or API lookups.

use_cases.title: Module pattern
use_cases.description: Before ES modules, IIFEs returned a public API while keeping helpers private; the idea still appears in SDK code.

demonstration.description: Run the loop question with var and let, then fix the var version with an IIFE. The difference comes from how many bindings of i exist, not from timing.
demonstration.output:
var 3
var 3
var 3
let 0
let 1
let 2
iife 0
iife 1
iife 2

takeaways: JavaScript is lexically scoped: where a function is written decides what it can see.
let and const are block-scoped and sit in the temporal dead zone until their declaration runs.
Function declarations are hoisted with their body; var is hoisted as undefined.
A closure keeps references to outer variables alive after the outer function returns.
Closures capture variables, not snapshots, which explains the var loop bug.
Closures give private state, factories, memoization and middleware configuration.

interview.question: What is the difference between var, let and const?
interview.answer: var is function-scoped, hoisted and initialised to undefined, and can be redeclared. let and const are block-scoped and stay in the temporal dead zone until declared. let can be reassigned; const cannot, although the object it refers to can be mutated.
interview.explanation: Cover scope, hoisting behaviour and reassignment. Mentioning that const does not make objects immutable (use Object.freeze for a shallow freeze) is a common follow-up.

interview.question: What is hoisting?
interview.answer: Before executing a scope, the engine creates bindings for all its declarations. Function declarations are fully available early, var bindings start as undefined, and let/const/class bindings exist but are uninitialised, so accessing them early throws a ReferenceError.
interview.explanation: Avoid saying code is 'moved to the top'; describe the creation phase of the execution context. Name the temporal dead zone.

interview.question: What is a closure? Give a practical example.
interview.answer: A closure is a function together with references to the variables of the scope where it was created. For example, a counter factory returns increment and value functions that share a private count variable which outside code cannot touch.
interview.explanation: Strong answers give a real use: middleware factories, debounce, memoization or React event handlers, and mention that each factory call gets its own environment.

interview.question: Why does a for loop with var and setTimeout print the same number three times, and how do you fix it?
interview.answer: var creates a single function-scoped i shared by every callback; by the time the callbacks run the loop has finished and i equals 3. Using let creates a new binding per iteration; alternatively wrap the body in an IIFE that receives i as a parameter.
interview.explanation: Interviewers want the reason (one binding vs per-iteration bindings and callbacks running after the loop), not just the fix.

interview.question: Can closures cause memory leaks? How?
interview.answer: Yes. Variables referenced by a live closure cannot be garbage-collected. A long-lived event listener or timer that closes over a large array or a detached DOM node keeps that data in memory. Removing listeners, clearing timers and not capturing more than needed prevent this.
interview.explanation: This advanced question checks that you understand closures are retained references. Mention cleanup in React useEffect as a real-world example.

interview.question: Implement once(fn).
interview.answer: function once(fn) { let called = false, result; return function (...args) { if (!called) { called = true; result = fn.apply(this, args); } return result; }; }
interview.explanation: Two closure variables track state. Using fn.apply(this, args) preserves the caller's this and arguments, a detail interviewers notice.

practice.title: Counter factory with private state
practice.objective: Use closures to build independent counters whose state can only be changed through returned methods.
practice.statement:
Implement makeCounter(start, step) that returns an object with inc, dec, reset and get methods closing over a private count. Then process commands, one per line:
- create <name> <start> <step>: create (or replace) a counter.
- inc <name> / dec <name>: add or subtract step.
- reset <name>: set the count back to start.
- get <name>: print <name>=<count>.
If a command (other than create) names a counter that does not exist, print error: unknown counter <name>.
practice.input_format: One command per line in the global string stdin. Blank lines are ignored.
practice.output_format: One line for every get command or error, in order.

example.input:
create a 5 1
inc a
inc a
get a
create b 0 10
inc b
dec a
get a
get b

constraints: Do not store counts in a shared global object; keep each count inside its closure.
explanation: makeCounter declares count with let; the four returned methods close over count, start and step.
Each call to makeCounter creates a new environment, so counters a and b never share state.
A Map stores the counter objects by name; creating the same name again replaces the old closure.
For every other command, look up the counter, print an error if missing, otherwise call the method or print the value.

inc a
inc a
get a
create b 0 10
inc b
dec a
get a
get b

get x
create x 3 2
inc x
get x

create c 100 25
dec c
dec c
get c

get c
inc d
tests.output:
c=50
c=100
error: unknown counter d

inc a

quiz.question: What does this code print?
quiz.explanation: var creates one shared i. The callbacks run after the loop ends, when i is 3.

quiz.question: What happens when this code runs?
quiz.explanation: total is hoisted but uninitialised; reading it inside the temporal dead zone throws a ReferenceError.

quiz.question: Which statement about closures is correct?
options: A closure's variables are deleted when the outer function returns
A closure captures references to outer variables, so later changes are visible
A closure copies outer variables at creation time
Closures only exist for arrow functions
quiz.explanation: Closures hold references to the variables themselves, which stay alive while the inner function is reachable.

quiz.question: Two counters are created with const a = makeCounter(); const b = makeCounter(); then a.increment() is called twice. What is b.value() if makeCounter declares let count = 0 inside itself?
quiz.explanation: Each call to makeCounter creates a new environment with its own count, so b is unaffected.

quiz.question: An Express app uses app.use(requireRole('admin')) where requireRole returns (req, res, next) => {...}. How does the inner function know the required role?
options: It closes over the role parameter of requireRole
It reads a global variable named role
The role is passed as the fourth middleware argument
Express stores it on req.role automatically
quiz.explanation: The returned middleware is a closure over requireRole's parameter, a common factory pattern.

lesson.title: The this Keyword, Prototypes and ES6 Classes
objectives: Apply the four binding rules that decide the value of this, plus the arrow-function exception.
Use call, apply and bind and explain when each is useful.
Explain the prototype chain and how property lookup and shadowing work.
Relate ES6 classes, extends and super to the prototypes underneath them.
Diagnose the 'lost this' bug when a method is passed as a callback.
lesson.definition: this is a special value set when a function is called; it usually refers to the object the function was called on. Every JavaScript object also has an internal link to another object, its prototype, and property lookups that fail on the object continue along this prototype chain. ES6 classes are cleaner syntax over the same prototype mechanism.

theory.heading: How this is decided: call-site rules
theory.body: For a normal function, this is not fixed when the function is written; it is decided by how the function is called. The rules are checked in priority order. Getting this right matters in Node and React code, where methods are often passed around as callbacks and lose their object.
points: new binding: new User() sets this to the freshly created object.
Explicit binding: fn.call(obj, a, b), fn.apply(obj, [a, b]) or fn.bind(obj) sets this to obj.
Implicit binding: user.greet() sets this to user, the object before the dot.
Default binding: a plain call greet() gives undefined in strict mode (modules and classes are strict) or the global object in sloppy mode.

theory.heading: Arrow functions and lexical this
theory.body: Arrow functions do not have their own this. They use the this of the scope in which they were defined, and call, apply or bind cannot change it. This makes arrows ideal for callbacks inside methods, such as array.map inside a class method, but wrong as object methods that need the object, because an arrow defined in an object literal takes this from the surrounding module or function, not the object.
points: Use arrows for callbacks that should keep the outer this.
Do not use arrows for object methods or prototype methods that rely on this.
Arrow functions also lack arguments and cannot be used with new.

theory.heading: The prototype chain
theory.body: When you read obj.prop, the engine checks obj's own properties first. If the property is missing, it follows obj's [[Prototype]] link (available through Object.getPrototypeOf) and checks there, continuing until it finds the property or reaches null, in which case the result is undefined. Writing obj.prop = value normally creates an own property on obj, shadowing the inherited one without changing the prototype. Methods placed on a prototype are shared by every instance, which saves memory.
points: Object.create(proto) makes a new object whose prototype is proto.
obj.hasOwnProperty(key) or Object.hasOwn(obj, key) tells own from inherited properties.
Arrays inherit from Array.prototype, which inherits from Object.prototype, whose prototype is null.

theory.heading: ES6 classes are prototypes with better syntax
theory.body: class User { greet() {} } creates a constructor function User and puts greet on User.prototype. extends links Child.prototype to Parent.prototype, and super(...) must be called in a derived constructor before using this. Class bodies run in strict mode. Fields declared as handle = () => {} are created per instance and capture this lexically, which is a common way to avoid binding issues in React class components and event emitters.
points: typeof User is 'function'; classes are not a new object model.
Static methods live on the class itself, not on instances.
#private fields are truly private and are not on the prototype.

theory.heading: The lost-this bug
theory.body: const fn = user.greet; fn(); separates the method from its object, so the call-site rule becomes the default binding and this is undefined in strict code. The same happens with setTimeout(user.greet, 100) or passing a class method as an Express route handler or React onClick. Fixes are bind in the constructor, an arrow wrapper () => user.greet(), or a class field arrow function.
points: The function is the same; only the call site changed.
bind returns a new function with this permanently fixed.

example.title: Prototype-based inheritance with a class
example.body: Admin extends User. An admin instance finds describe on User.prototype through the chain, while canDelete is found on Admin.prototype. The extracted method shows the lost-this bug and its fix with bind.

use_cases.title: Mongoose models
use_cases.description: Mongoose schema methods are added to the model's prototype, and they use this to reach the document, which is why they must be normal functions, not arrows.

use_cases.title: Express controllers as classes
use_cases.description: Passing controller.getUser as a route handler loses this unless the method is bound or written as a class-field arrow.

use_cases.title: Custom error classes
use_cases.description: class NotFoundError extends Error sets name and status so a central error handler can respond correctly.

use_cases.title: Event emitters
use_cases.description: Node's EventEmitter calls listeners with this set to the emitter for normal functions, but not for arrow listeners.

demonstration.description: Call one function four different ways and observe how this changes. The module is in strict mode, so a plain call gives undefined.

takeaways: this depends on the call site: new, explicit, implicit, then default.
Arrow functions take this from their defining scope and ignore call/apply/bind.
Property lookup walks the prototype chain until it reaches null.
Assigning a property creates an own property that shadows the inherited one.
Classes are syntax over constructor functions and prototypes.
Passing a method as a callback loses this; fix it with bind or an arrow wrapper.

interview.question: How is the value of this determined in JavaScript?
interview.answer: By the call site. With new it is the new object; with call, apply or bind it is the given object; with obj.method() it is obj; otherwise it is undefined in strict mode or the global object in sloppy mode. Arrow functions ignore these rules and use the enclosing scope's this.
interview.explanation: List the rules in priority order and add the arrow exception. A quick example of each rule shows real understanding.

interview.question: What is the difference between call, apply and bind?
interview.answer: call invokes the function immediately with a given this and arguments listed individually; apply does the same with arguments as an array; bind does not invoke but returns a new function with this (and optionally leading arguments) permanently fixed.
interview.explanation: Mention a use for bind such as fixing a callback, and that a bound function cannot be re-bound.

interview.question: Explain prototypal inheritance.
interview.answer: Each object has an internal prototype link. When a property is not found on the object, the engine looks it up on the prototype, then the prototype's prototype, until null. Shared methods live on the prototype, so all instances reuse them.
interview.explanation: Strong answers mention Object.create, Object.getPrototypeOf and shadowing, and contrast this with copying in classical inheritance.

interview.question: Are ES6 classes different from constructor functions?
interview.answer: They use the same prototype model, but classes add guarantees: the body is strict, the class cannot be called without new, methods are non-enumerable, extends and super wire up the chain, and private #fields are supported.
interview.explanation: Interviewers check that you know classes are syntactic sugar but not identical, and can name the practical differences.

interview.question: Why should a Mongoose schema method not be an arrow function?
interview.answer: Mongoose calls the method with this set to the document. An arrow function ignores that binding and uses the this of the module scope, so this.name would be undefined.
interview.explanation: Links today's theory to MERN code; the same reasoning applies to pre-save hooks.

practice.title: Trace the prototype chain
practice.objective: Build objects with Object.create and report where a property is found during prototype lookup.
practice.statement:
Process commands:
- obj <name> <parent|null> [key=value ...]: create an object whose prototype is the named parent object (or null) with the given own properties.
- set <name> <key=value>: assign a property on that object (it becomes an own property).
- get <name> <key>: print <name>.<key> = <value> (own) if the property is the object's own, <name>.<key> = <value> (from <owner>) if it was inherited from object <owner>, or <name>.<key> = undefined if no object in the chain has it.
Use real prototypes: create objects with Object.create and walk the chain with Object.getPrototypeOf.
practice.input_format: One command per line. A parent is always defined before its children.

example.input:
obj animal null speak=generic legs=4
obj dog animal speak=woof
obj puppy dog age=1
get puppy speak
get puppy legs
get puppy fly
set puppy speak=yip
get puppy speak
get dog speak
example.output:
puppy.speak = woof (from dog)
puppy.legs = 4 (from animal)
puppy.fly = undefined
puppy.speak = yip (own)
dog.speak = woof (own)

constraints: Names, keys and values contain no spaces or '=' characters other than the separator.
Objects created with parent null must not inherit anything (not even toString).
explanation: Object.create(parent) sets the new object's prototype; Object.create(null) gives an object with no prototype at all.
Own properties are assigned directly, so later assignments shadow inherited values instead of changing the parent.
ownerOf checks own properties with Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call (safe even for null-prototype objects), then moves up with Object.getPrototypeOf.
obj[key] performs the engine's own lookup; ownerOf only identifies which object supplied the value.

quiz.question: What is logged in an ES module (strict mode)?
quiz.explanation: fn() is a plain call, so this is undefined in strict mode; optional chaining returns undefined instead of throwing.

quiz.question: Which method returns a new function with this permanently fixed, without calling it?
quiz.explanation: bind returns a new bound function; call and apply invoke the function immediately.

quiz.question: A class method passed as onClick={this.handleSave} throws 'Cannot read properties of undefined'. What is the most direct fix?
options: Rename the method to start with on
Convert the class to use var
Define handleSave as a class-field arrow function or bind it in the constructor
quiz.explanation: Passing the method detaches it from the instance. Binding or a class-field arrow keeps this pointing at the instance.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.explanation: Assigning role on admin creates an own property that shadows the inherited one; base is not changed.

quiz.question: Where does a method defined in a class body, such as greet() {}, live?
options: On the class's prototype object, shared by instances
On each instance as an own property
On the class constructor as a static property
quiz.explanation: Class methods are placed on ClassName.prototype; only class fields are created per instance.

lesson.title: Promises, async/await and Promise Combinators
objectives: Explain the three promise states and how then/catch/finally chains pass values and errors.
Rewrite promise chains with async/await and handle errors with try/catch.
Choose between sequential and parallel awaiting for independent work.
Compare Promise.all, allSettled, race and any and pick the right one for a scenario.
Avoid common bugs: forgotten await, await inside forEach and unhandled rejections.
lesson.definition: A Promise is an object representing the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. It starts pending and settles exactly once, either fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason. async functions always return a promise, and await pauses the async function until a promise settles, letting asynchronous code read like synchronous code.

theory.heading: Why promises replaced callbacks
theory.body: Node's original style passed a callback (err, result) to every asynchronous function. Nested callbacks grow rightwards ('callback hell'), error handling must be repeated at each level, and nothing stops a buggy library from calling your callback twice. A promise settles only once, errors propagate down a chain to the nearest catch, and promises can be composed with combinators. Modern Node APIs such as fs/promises, the MongoDB driver and fetch all return promises.
points: States: pending, then fulfilled or rejected; a settled promise never changes.
then(onFulfilled, onRejected) returns a new promise, which makes chaining possible.
Returning a value from then passes it on; throwing (or returning a rejected promise) moves to the next catch.

theory.heading: async/await
theory.body: An async function always returns a promise: a returned value fulfils it and a thrown error rejects it. Inside, await expression waits for the promise to settle, then returns its value or throws its rejection reason, so ordinary try/catch/finally works. await only pauses the current async function; the rest of the program, including other requests in an Express server, keeps running.
points: Forgetting await gives you a pending Promise object instead of the data.
Errors from awaited promises are caught by the surrounding try/catch.
Top-level await is allowed in ES modules.

theory.heading: Sequential vs parallel
theory.body: Writing const a = await getUser(); const b = await getOrders(); runs the calls one after another, so the total time is the sum. If the calls do not depend on each other, start both first and await them together with Promise.all, so the total time is roughly the slowest one. In an API endpoint that loads a profile, its orders and its notifications, this can cut latency dramatically. Use sequential awaits only when a later call needs an earlier result.
points: array.forEach(async ...) does not wait; use for...of with await for sequential work.
Use Promise.all(items.map(async ...)) for parallel work, with a concurrency limit for large lists.

theory.heading: The four combinators
theory.body: Promise combinators take an iterable of promises and return one promise. They differ in what they wait for and when they short-circuit. Knowing these precisely is a frequent interview check because choosing the wrong one either hides failures or fails a whole page because of one optional widget.
points: Promise.all: fulfils with all values in input order; rejects as soon as any input rejects.
Promise.allSettled: never rejects; waits for all and returns {status, value|reason} objects.
Promise.race: settles like the first input to settle, fulfilled or rejected (useful for timeouts).
Promise.any: fulfils with the first fulfilment; rejects with an AggregateError only if all reject.

theory.heading: Error handling and unhandled rejections
theory.body: A rejected promise with no handler triggers an unhandledRejection event. Since Node 15 the default behaviour is to crash the process, which is safer than silently continuing. In Express 4, an error thrown inside an async route handler is not passed to the error middleware automatically, so you must wrap handlers or call next(err); Express 5 forwards rejected promises from handlers to the error middleware itself.
points: Always end a chain with catch or wrap awaits in try/catch.
Note that Promise.all does not cancel the other operations when one fails; use AbortController for cancellation.

example.title: Parallel loading in an API handler
example.body: The dashboard needs the user and their orders, which are independent. Starting both requests before awaiting halves the latency compared to awaiting them one by one. The optional recommendations call uses allSettled so its failure does not break the page.

use_cases.title: Aggregating microservice calls
use_cases.description: An Express endpoint fetches profile, cart and offers in parallel with Promise.all to keep response time low.

use_cases.title: Optional widgets
use_cases.description: Promise.allSettled loads non-critical sections so one failing service shows a fallback instead of a 500 error.

use_cases.title: Timeouts for LLM or third-party calls
use_cases.description: Promise.race between the request and a timer rejects slow calls; AbortController then cancels the request.

use_cases.title: Fastest mirror or region
use_cases.description: Promise.any accepts the first successful response from several replicas and only fails if all fail.

use_cases.title: Database transactions and migrations
use_cases.description: Sequential awaits in a for...of loop keep steps in order when each depends on the previous one.

demonstration.description: Compare how combinators settle for the same three tasks: a fulfils after 30 ms, b rejects after 10 ms, c fulfils after 20 ms.
demonstration.output:
all rejected b-error
race rejected b-error
any c
allSettled fulfilled,rejected,fulfilled

takeaways: A promise settles once: fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason.
async functions return promises; await unwraps them and throws on rejection.
Independent awaits should run in parallel with Promise.all.
all fails fast, allSettled never rejects, race takes the first settlement, any takes the first success.
forEach does not await async callbacks; use for...of or Promise.all with map.
Unhandled rejections crash modern Node, so every chain needs error handling.

interview.question: What is a Promise and what states can it be in?
interview.answer: A Promise represents a value that will be available later. It is pending until it settles once, either fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason, after which its state never changes.
interview.explanation: Mention that then returns a new promise, enabling chaining, and that settlement is one-time, unlike callbacks that might be called twice.

interview.question: What is the difference between Promise.all and Promise.allSettled?
interview.answer: Promise.all fulfils with an array of values when every input fulfils and rejects immediately when any input rejects. Promise.allSettled always waits for every input and fulfils with objects describing each outcome.
interview.explanation: Give a scenario: use all when every result is required, allSettled for optional or independent tasks such as sending notifications.

interview.question: How would you make three independent database calls faster in an async function?
interview.answer: Start all three without awaiting, then await Promise.all on them, so they run concurrently and the total time approaches the slowest call instead of the sum.
interview.explanation: Strong candidates also mention limits: very large arrays need a concurrency cap so the database connection pool is not flooded.

interview.question: Why does await inside array.forEach not work as expected?
interview.answer: forEach ignores the promises returned by its async callback, so the outer function continues immediately and errors become unhandled. Use for...of to await sequentially or Promise.all(array.map(...)) for parallel execution.
interview.explanation: A very common bug in Node scripts and seeders; naming both alternatives shows practical experience.

interview.question: How do you implement a timeout for a slow API call?
interview.answer: Race the call against a promise that rejects after N milliseconds using Promise.race, or better, pass an AbortSignal (for example AbortSignal.timeout(5000)) to fetch so the underlying request is actually cancelled.
interview.explanation: The advanced point is that race alone only stops waiting; it does not stop the request. AbortController cancels it.

practice.title: Predict the Promise combinator result
practice.objective: Model exactly how Promise.all, allSettled, race and any settle given task outcomes and timings.
practice.statement:
The first line names a combinator: all, allSettled, race or any. Each following line describes one task: <name> <ok|fail> <delayMs> <value>. A task fulfils (ok) or rejects (fail) with <value> after <delayMs>. Tasks with equal delays settle in input order. Print what the combinator produces and when it settles:
- all: fulfilled: [v1,v2,...] in input order at the latest delay, or rejected: <reason> of the earliest rejection at that rejection's time.
- allSettled: one line per task in input order, <name>: fulfilled <value> or <name>: rejected <value>, settling at the latest delay.
- race: fulfilled: <value> or rejected: <value> for the first task to settle.
- any: fulfilled: <value> for the first fulfilment; if every task rejects, rejected: AggregateError [r1,r2,...] in input order at the latest delay.
The final line is always at <ms>ms.
practice.input_format: Line 1: combinator name. Following lines: name status delay value.

example.input:
all
a ok 100 user
b ok 50 orders
c fail 80 timeout

constraints: 1 to 20 tasks; delays are non-negative integers.
Do not use real timers; compute the result from the rules.
explanation: Parse each task and remember its input position, which is used both for result order and for breaking ties in timing.
Sort a copy of the tasks by delay to know the order in which they settle.
all short-circuits on the earliest rejection; otherwise it reports values in input order (not completion order) at the latest delay.
allSettled always waits for every task; race takes whatever settles first; any skips rejections and only fails with an AggregateError when all reject.

tests.input:
all
a ok 100 user
b ok 50 orders
c fail 80 timeout

all
a ok 30 x
b ok 10 y

allSettled
a ok 20 1
b fail 40 err
tests.output:
a: fulfilled 1
b: rejected err
at 40ms

tests.input:
race
a ok 50 slow
b fail 10 boom

any
a fail 10 e1
b ok 60 v
c ok 30 w

any
a fail 10 e1
b fail 5 e2

quiz.question: Which combinator should you use to send emails to 50 users and then report how many succeeded and failed?
quiz.explanation: allSettled waits for every promise and reports each outcome without rejecting on the first failure.

quiz.question: What does this log?
quiz.code:
async function f() { return 42; }
console.log(typeof f(), f() instanceof Promise);
quiz.explanation: An async function always returns a Promise, which is an object, even when the body returns a plain value.

quiz.question: An endpoint awaits getUser(), then getOrders(), then getAddresses(), each taking 200 ms and all independent. What change most reduces latency?
options: Wrap each await in its own try/catch
Move them into a forEach loop
quiz.explanation: Independent calls should start together; Promise.all reduces total time from about 600 ms to about 200 ms.

quiz.question: When does Promise.any reject?
options: Only when every input rejects, with an AggregateError
When any input takes longer than 1 second
quiz.explanation: Promise.any ignores rejections while any input might still fulfil, and rejects with an AggregateError only if all fail.

quiz.question: items.forEach(async (item) => { await save(item); }); console.log('done'); What is the problem?
options: 'done' prints before the saves finish and their errors are not handled
save runs twice for each item
forEach throws because async callbacks are not allowed
quiz.explanation: forEach ignores the returned promises, so execution continues immediately and rejections go unhandled.

questions.question: What is the difference between var, let and const?
questions.answer: var is function-scoped, hoisted and initialised to undefined, and can be redeclared. let and const are block-scoped and stay in the temporal dead zone until declared. let can be reassigned; const cannot, although the object it refers to can be mutated.
questions.explanation: Cover scope, hoisting behaviour and reassignment. Mentioning that const does not make objects immutable (use Object.freeze for a shallow freeze) is a common follow-up.

questions.question: What is hoisting?
questions.answer: Before executing a scope, the engine creates bindings for all its declarations. Function declarations are fully available early, var bindings start as undefined, and let/const/class bindings exist but are uninitialised, so accessing them early throws a ReferenceError.
questions.explanation: Avoid saying code is 'moved to the top'; describe the creation phase of the execution context. Name the temporal dead zone.

questions.question: What is a closure? Give a practical example.
questions.answer: A closure is a function together with references to the variables of the scope where it was created. For example, a counter factory returns increment and value functions that share a private count variable which outside code cannot touch.
questions.explanation: Strong answers give a real use: middleware factories, debounce, memoization or React event handlers, and mention that each factory call gets its own environment.

questions.question: Why does a for loop with var and setTimeout print the same number three times, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: var creates a single function-scoped i shared by every callback; by the time the callbacks run the loop has finished and i equals 3. Using let creates a new binding per iteration; alternatively wrap the body in an IIFE that receives i as a parameter.
questions.explanation: Interviewers want the reason (one binding vs per-iteration bindings and callbacks running after the loop), not just the fix.

questions.question: Can closures cause memory leaks? How?
questions.answer: Yes. Variables referenced by a live closure cannot be garbage-collected. A long-lived event listener or timer that closes over a large array or a detached DOM node keeps that data in memory. Removing listeners, clearing timers and not capturing more than needed prevent this.
questions.explanation: This advanced question checks that you understand closures are retained references. Mention cleanup in React useEffect as a real-world example.

questions.question: Implement once(fn).
questions.answer: function once(fn) { let called = false, result; return function (...args) { if (!called) { called = true; result = fn.apply(this, args); } return result; }; }
questions.explanation: Two closure variables track state. Using fn.apply(this, args) preserves the caller's this and arguments, a detail interviewers notice.

questions.topic: The this Keyword, Prototypes and ES6 Classes
questions.question: How is the value of this determined in JavaScript?
questions.answer: By the call site. With new it is the new object; with call, apply or bind it is the given object; with obj.method() it is obj; otherwise it is undefined in strict mode or the global object in sloppy mode. Arrow functions ignore these rules and use the enclosing scope's this.
questions.explanation: List the rules in priority order and add the arrow exception. A quick example of each rule shows real understanding.

questions.topic: The this Keyword, Prototypes and ES6 Classes
questions.question: What is the difference between call, apply and bind?
questions.answer: call invokes the function immediately with a given this and arguments listed individually; apply does the same with arguments as an array; bind does not invoke but returns a new function with this (and optionally leading arguments) permanently fixed.
questions.explanation: Mention a use for bind such as fixing a callback, and that a bound function cannot be re-bound.

questions.topic: The this Keyword, Prototypes and ES6 Classes
questions.question: Explain prototypal inheritance.
questions.answer: Each object has an internal prototype link. When a property is not found on the object, the engine looks it up on the prototype, then the prototype's prototype, until null. Shared methods live on the prototype, so all instances reuse them.
questions.explanation: Strong answers mention Object.create, Object.getPrototypeOf and shadowing, and contrast this with copying in classical inheritance.

questions.topic: The this Keyword, Prototypes and ES6 Classes
questions.question: Are ES6 classes different from constructor functions?
questions.answer: They use the same prototype model, but classes add guarantees: the body is strict, the class cannot be called without new, methods are non-enumerable, extends and super wire up the chain, and private #fields are supported.
questions.explanation: Interviewers check that you know classes are syntactic sugar but not identical, and can name the practical differences.

questions.topic: The this Keyword, Prototypes and ES6 Classes
questions.question: Why should a Mongoose schema method not be an arrow function?
questions.answer: Mongoose calls the method with this set to the document. An arrow function ignores that binding and uses the this of the module scope, so this.name would be undefined.
questions.explanation: Links today's theory to MERN code; the same reasoning applies to pre-save hooks.

days.title: JavaScript Scope, Hoisting and Closures
days.focus: Scope is the set of rules that decides where a variable can be accessed. JavaScript uses lexical scope: a function can see the variables of the place where it was written, not where it is called. A closure is a function bundled with references to the variables of its surrounding scope, so it can keep reading and updating them even after the outer function has returned.
objectives: Explain global, function and block scope and how the scope chain resolves a variable.
Describe hoisting for var, let, const, function declarations and the temporal dead zone.
Define a closure and explain why an inner function keeps access to outer variables.
Use closures for private state, factories and once/memoize helpers.
Predict the output of the classic loop-with-setTimeout interview question.
days.assignment:
Implement makeCounter(start, step) that returns an object with inc, dec, reset and get methods closing over a private count. Then process commands, one per line:
- create <name> <start> <step>: create (or replace) a counter.
- inc <name> / dec <name>: add or subtract step.
- reset <name>: set the count back to start.
- get <name>: print <name>=<count>.
If a command (other than create) names a counter that does not exist, print error: unknown counter <name>.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: JavaScript is lexically scoped: where a function is written decides what it can see.
let and const are block-scoped and sit in the temporal dead zone until their declaration runs.
Function declarations are hoisted with their body; var is hoisted as undefined.
A closure keeps references to outer variables alive after the outer function returns.
Closures capture variables, not snapshots, which explains the var loop bug.
Closures give private state, factories, memoization and middleware configuration.

days.title: The this Keyword, Prototypes and ES6 Classes
days.focus: this is a special value set when a function is called; it usually refers to the object the function was called on. Every JavaScript object also has an internal link to another object, its prototype, and property lookups that fail on the object continue along this prototype chain. ES6 classes are cleaner syntax over the same prototype mechanism.
objectives: Apply the four binding rules that decide the value of this, plus the arrow-function exception.
Use call, apply and bind and explain when each is useful.
Explain the prototype chain and how property lookup and shadowing work.
Relate ES6 classes, extends and super to the prototypes underneath them.
Diagnose the 'lost this' bug when a method is passed as a callback.
days.assignment:
Process commands:
- obj <name> <parent|null> [key=value ...]: create an object whose prototype is the named parent object (or null) with the given own properties.
- set <name> <key=value>: assign a property on that object (it becomes an own property).
- get <name> <key>: print <name>.<key> = <value> (own) if the property is the object's own, <name>.<key> = <value> (from <owner>) if it was inherited from object <owner>, or <name>.<key> = undefined if no object in the chain has it.
Use real prototypes: create objects with Object.create and walk the chain with Object.getPrototypeOf.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: this depends on the call site: new, explicit, implicit, then default.
Arrow functions take this from their defining scope and ignore call/apply/bind.
Property lookup walks the prototype chain until it reaches null.
Assigning a property creates an own property that shadows the inherited one.
Classes are syntax over constructor functions and prototypes.
Passing a method as a callback loses this; fix it with bind or an arrow wrapper.

days.title: Promises, async/await and Promise Combinators

It starts pending and settles exactly once, either fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason. async functions always return a promise, and await pauses the async function until a promise settles, letting asynchronous code read like synchronous code.
